summary: Defines the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol, a transport protocol offering two-way unicast connections of congestion-controlled but unreliable datagrams. It suits applications that move fairly large amounts of data and want control over the tradeoff between timeliness and reliability. It is standards-track and was later updated by RFC 5595, RFC 5596, RFC 6335, and RFC 6773.

eli5.summary: Like TCP, it keeps a connection and slows down when the road is crowded, but it does not resend lost messages. That suits live video, where old data is useless.

subtitle: A transport protocol that keeps a connection and plays fair with congestion, but never resends lost data.

tldr.problem: Streaming and similar applications want timely delivery, not reliable in-order delivery. TCP can delay data arbitrarily, while UDP leaves every application to build its own congestion control.
tldr.mechanism: DCCP sets up a connection with a three-way handshake, numbers every packet, and acknowledges packets so the sender can learn about loss and ECN marks. The two directions each use a negotiated congestion control mechanism (CCID), and no lost data is retransmitted.
tldr.outcome: Applications get congestion-controlled, unreliable datagram flows with built-in ECN support and a choice of congestion control behavior. The RFC was later updated by RFC 5595, RFC 5596, RFC 6335 and RFC 6773.

today: RFC 4340 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 5595, RFC 5596, RFC 6335 and RFC 6773. The congestion control details are in the CCID profiles RFC 4341 and RFC 4342.

sections.title: What DCCP Provides and Why
sections.content:
The Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP) is a transport protocol for bidirectional, unicast connections of congestion-controlled, unreliable datagrams. It is meant for applications that move fairly large amounts of data and want control over the tradeoff between timeliness and reliability, such as streaming media.

The RFC positions it between two older protocols. TCP gives reliable in-order delivery, but that and its congestion control can cause arbitrarily long delays. UDP avoids long delays, but any UDP application that wants congestion control must build it itself. DCCP supplies the congestion control, including support for Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN), without the arbitrary delays.

The RFC lists what DCCP offers: unreliable datagram flows, reliable handshakes for setup and teardown, reliable negotiation of options (including the congestion control mechanism), mechanisms that let servers avoid holding state for unacknowledged connection attempts, acknowledgements that report loss and ECN information, and Path MTU discovery.

A design goal was to give streaming UDP applications little reason not to switch. DCCP therefore keeps overhead low in header size and in end-host state, and leaves things like forward error correction, semi-reliability and multiple streams to be layered on top. The RFC describes it as TCP minus bytestream semantics and reliability, or as UDP plus congestion control, handshakes and acknowledgements.
sections.eli5: Some programs, like video calls, care more about speed than about getting every piece. DCCP lets them send pieces quickly while still being polite about not jamming up the network.

sections.title: Packets and the Generic Header
sections.content:
Every DCCP packet starts with a fixed-size generic header, followed by extra fixed fields that depend on the packet type, then options, then application data. The whole DCCP header can be from 12 to 1020 bytes long.

The generic header carries the source and destination ports (placed where TCP and UDP put theirs), a Data Offset, a 4-bit CCVal used by the sender's congestion control mechanism, a 4-bit Checksum Coverage field, a 16-bit checksum, a 4-bit Type, and the sequence number. The X bit chooses the form: with X=1 the sequence number is 48 bits and the header is 16 bytes; with X=0 only the low 24 bits are sent and the header is 12 bytes.

Ten packet types do the work. A connection begins with DCCP-Request and DCCP-Response, carries data in DCCP-Data, DCCP-Ack and DCCP-DataAck, and ends with DCCP-CloseReq, DCCP-Close and DCCP-Reset. DCCP-Sync and DCCP-SyncAck resynchronize endpoints after bursts of loss. Because the packet type is a single field, there is no way to send an unexpected flag combination like TCP's SYN+FIN+ACK+RST.

Receivers MUST ignore packets with a reserved type. All packets other than DCCP-Request and DCCP-Data carry an Acknowledgement Number, which is 48 bits when X=1. Options follow the header; their total length must be a multiple of 32 bits, so Padding options fill the gap, and unknown options MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: Every DCCP packet starts with a label saying where it came from, where it is going, what kind of packet it is and its place in line, like a numbered ticket on a parcel.

sections.title: Feature Negotiation
sections.content:
A DCCP feature is a connection attribute on whose value both endpoints agree. Each feature number applies to each endpoint separately, so the client and server can end up with different values for the same feature number. Features include which congestion control mechanism each direction uses.

Agreement is reached with four options: Change L, Confirm L, Change R and Confirm R. The L options are sent by the endpoint where the feature lives and the R options by the other endpoint. A Change option starts a negotiation and is retransmitted until some response arrives; a Confirm option completes it and is never sent except in reply to a Change. Negotiation usually happens in the opening handshake but can begin at any time.

Two reconciliation rules exist. With server-priority, each side lists values in preference order and the result is the first entry in the server's list that also appears in the client's list. With non-negotiable, the feature location simply announces a value, and the other side must accept any valid value. An invalid Change gets an empty Confirm option back.

Table 4 of the RFC defines features 1 to 9: Congestion Control ID, Allow Short Seqnos, Sequence Window, ECN Incapable, Ack Ratio, Send Ack Vector, Send NDP Count, Minimum Checksum Coverage and Check Data Checksum. Feature numbers 128 to 255 are left for CCID-specific use.

The Mandatory option marks the option after it as required. If the receiver cannot process that option, it MUST reset the connection with Reset Code 6.
sections.eli5: Before playing a game, two kids agree on the rules. DCCP lets the two computers agree on how they will share the network, and keeps asking until the other side answers.

sections.title: Opening, Running and Closing a Connection
sections.content:
A DCCP connection has a client, which starts it, and a server, which waits. Setup is a three-way handshake. The client sends DCCP-Request carrying a 32-bit Service Code that names the application-level service wanted, and usually some feature negotiation. The server answers with DCCP-Response, and the client replies with a DCCP-Ack or DCCP-DataAck. The Service Code lets middleboxes recognize an application on a nonstandard port, and a server rejects an unknown one with Reset Code 8, Bad Service Code.

To avoid holding state for half-open connections, the server may put its handshake state into an opaque Init Cookie option, much like TCP SYN cookies. The client must echo it back until the handshake is confirmed. After receiving the Response, the client sits in the PARTOPEN state and must send data in DCCP-DataAck packets until it knows the server has seen one of its packets.

Closing is a handshake too. A server that does not want to hold the TIMEWAIT state sends DCCP-CloseReq; the client answers DCCP-Close; the server answers DCCP-Reset with Reset Code 1, Closed. Either side may instead send DCCP-Close directly. Whoever receives the DCCP-Reset holds TIMEWAIT for 2MSL (4 minutes). Unlike TCP, which has FIN and RST, every DCCP connection ends with a DCCP-Reset, and the Reset Code tells clean from unclean endings.

Other differences from TCP noted in the RFC: there is no receive window, no simultaneous open and no half-closed states.
sections.eli5: It is like a phone call: one side dials, the other picks up and says hello, and the first says hello back. Hanging up also takes a short back-and-forth, and one side waits a bit so stray old messages do not confuse the next call.

sections.title: Sequence Numbers and Acknowledgements
sections.content:
DCCP sequence numbers count packets, not bytes. Every packet, including pure acknowledgements, increments the number by one, and arithmetic is modulo 2^48. Even effective retransmissions, such as a repeated DCCP-Request, get a new sequence number. That lets an endpoint detect network duplicates and even lost acknowledgements.

Since nothing is retransmitted, TCP-style cumulative acknowledgements make no sense. The Acknowledgement Number instead holds the greatest sequence number received on an acknowledgeable packet, meaning one whose header was successfully processed. Options such as Ack Vector fill in which packets in between were or were not received.

Each endpoint keeps a sequence-validity window, whose width is set by the Sequence Window feature (initial value 100, minimum 32). Packets outside it are sequence-invalid and not processed. Because a long burst of loss can push the sender's numbers out of the window, DCCP-Sync and DCCP-SyncAck exist to recover. A sequence-invalid packet elicits a DCCP-Sync, and implementations SHOULD rate limit these, for example to not more than eight per second.

Maximum packet size is tracked per connection from the path MTU, and senders should send packets as unfragmentable, using Path MTU discovery. The RFC suggests DCCP-Sync packets padded to size as safe probes, since losing one risks no application data.
sections.eli5: Every packet gets its own number, even the ones that just say thanks. If a number goes missing, the other side knows exactly which packet was lost, and nobody tries to resend it.

sections.title: Congestion Control and ECN
sections.content:
Congestion control is chosen by a one-byte CCID, negotiated using feature number 1. Each direction of the connection (each half-connection) can use a different CCID. New connections start with CCID 2. Two are defined: CCID 2 in RFC 4341 and CCID 3 in RFC 4342. Their detailed behavior lives in those profile documents, not in this RFC.

CCID 2 is TCP-like. The sender keeps a congestion window and halves it on each congestion event, which responds quickly to changing bandwidth but produces TCP's abrupt rate changes. Its acknowledgements use Ack Vector and arrive at about one per two packets. The RFC suggests it for applications that prefer maximum bandwidth over a steady rate.

CCID 3 is TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC), an equation-based mechanism with much lower variation in throughput, which suits streaming media. Here acknowledgements come at about one per round-trip time.

DCCP is fully ECN-aware. Senders SHOULD mark packets ECN-capable unless the receiver's ECN Incapable feature is on. To catch receivers that hide congestion, senders use ECN Nonces: they randomly pick between two ECN code points, and acknowledgement options echo the parity of the nonces received. A mismatch can trigger an aggression penalty, and an extreme case may end in a reset with Reset Code 11, Aggression Penalty, though the RFC says to treat that as a last resort.

A Slow Receiver option tells the sender the receiver is struggling, and the sender SHOULD NOT increase its rate for about one round-trip time. It is not a congestion signal.
sections.eli5: When many cars use one road, everyone has to ease off the gas. DCCP lets each program pick a style of easing off: stop-and-go like TCP, or a steady smooth speed.

sections.title: Checksums and Dropped Data
sections.content:
DCCP uses the same 16-bit one's complement checksum algorithm as TCP, computed over the header, options, an IP pseudoheader and, depending on the Checksum Coverage field (CsCov), some or all of the application data. Packets with an invalid checksum MUST be ignored, and their options MUST NOT be processed.

With CsCov = 0 the whole packet is covered. With values 1 to 15, the checksum covers the header plus the first (CsCov minus 1) times 4 bytes of data, so a value of 1 protects no application data. This lets applications that tolerate corruption ask links to reduce error protection, which can help on noisy links. The receiver's Minimum Checksum Coverage feature lets it refuse such packets, and by default only fully covered data is accepted. The RFC calls meanings of values other than 0 and 1 experimental.

An optional Data Checksum option adds a CRC-32c of the application data so the receiver can detect corruption in uncovered data.

The Data Dropped option lets a receiver report that a packet it acknowledged did not actually reach the application, and why, using Drop Codes such as 0 Protocol Constraints, 1 Application Not Listening, 2 Receive Buffer, 3 Corrupt and 7 Delivered Corrupt. TCP reports all loss the same way; this lets the two kinds of loss be told apart. Today, congestion control must still respond conservatively, as if such packets were ECN marked, until richer responses are standardized.
sections.eli5: A checksum is a quick check that the message was not smudged on the way. DCCP lets an app say it is fine with a smudge in the picture part of the message, as long as the address part is clean.

sections.title: Security and Middlebox Considerations
sections.content:
DCCP does not provide cryptographic security. Applications that need integrity, authentication, confidentiality or access control should use IPsec or some end-to-end security. DCCP also gives no protection against attackers who can snoop on data packets.

It does aim to stop attackers who cannot see the traffic. Hijacking a connection requires guessing valid sequence numbers, so initial sequence numbers must be chosen well, following TCP's strategies. Several mechanisms limit denial-of-service damage: the Init Cookie option, the DCCP-CloseReq packet that moves TIMEWAIT state to the client, the Application Not Listening drop code, limits on processing options that might cause a reset, and various rate limits.

The RFC also has advice for firewalls and address translators. The Service Code in a DCCP-Request shows which protocol a connection will use without relying on port numbers. Middleboxes should not act punitively toward options they do not understand, and should avoid adding or removing packets, since that would require rewriting acknowledgement options and ECN Nonce information. Partial checksums also interact badly with authentication, because an uncovered area may change in transit.
sections.eli5: DCCP locks the door against strangers who cannot see what is going on, but it does not put your letters in sealed envelopes. If you need secrets kept, you add a lock like IPsec yourself.

fields.name: Source Port
fields.desc: Port on the endpoint that sent the packet.

fields.name: Data Offset
fields.desc: Start of the application data, in 32-bit words.

fields.name: CCVal
fields.desc: Used by the sender's congestion control mechanism.

fields.name: CsCov
fields.desc: How much of the packet the checksum covers.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Internet checksum of the header, a pseudoheader and some or all data.

fields.name: Sequence Number (high bits)
fields.desc: Upper part of the 48-bit sequence number.

fields.name: Sequence Number (low bits)
fields.desc: Lower part of the sequence number.

items.label: DCCP-CloseReq
items.desc: Server asks the client to close.

items.label: DCCP-Close
items.desc: Closes the connection; elicits a Reset.

items.label: DCCP-Reset
items.desc: Ends the connection, cleanly or not.

items.label: DCCP-Sync
items.desc: Resynchronizes after a burst of loss.

messages.label: DCCP-Request
messages.note: Names the Service Code and opens feature negotiation.

messages.label: DCCP-Data / Ack / DataAck
messages.note: Data transfer; both directions may send.

messages.label: DCCP-CloseReq
messages.note: Server asks the client to hold TIMEWAIT.

messages.label: DCCP-Reset (Closed)
messages.note: Reset Code 1; client then holds TIMEWAIT for 2MSL.

items.desc: Packet arrived; any ECN code point other than CE.

items.desc: Packet arrived with ECN code point CE.
